units.title: Mama Put Comparisons: Figures of Speech

lessons.question: Consider the two lines: (i) 'He fights like a lion.' (ii) 'He is a lion in battle.' Which statement correctly identifies them?
options: Both are metaphors because both compare two things
(i) is a simile and (ii) is a metaphor
(i) is a metaphor and (ii) is a simile
Both are similes because both mention a lion
lessons.explanation: A simile compares openly using 'like' or 'as', while a metaphor says one thing simply IS the other. Line (i) uses 'like'; line (ii) does not.
lessons.hint: Look for the 'connector' words. Is there a 'like' or 'as' standing between the man and the lion, like a conductor between bus and passenger?

lessons.question: A poem about a village in mourning begins: 'The sun refused to rise.' What is the poet doing in this line?
options: Reporting that there was an eclipse that morning
Using a simile to compare the sun to a mourner
Personifying the sun to create a mood of gloom
Using hyperbole to show the day was very hot
lessons.explanation: Only a person can 'refuse' something, so the sun is given human will. This personification makes the whole world seem to share the village's sorrow.
lessons.hint: Can the sun really say 'I no go rise today'? Ask yourself who normally refuses things.

lessons.question: A mother shouts at her son: 'I have told you a million times to sweep this compound!' How should a student analyse 'a million times'?
options: As hyperbole showing her frustration at being ignored
As a literal count of how often she has spoken
As a writing error, since nobody speaks a million times
As an oxymoron joining two opposite ideas
lessons.explanation: This is hyperbole, a deliberate exaggeration. It is not meant to be counted; it stresses how tired she is of repeating herself.
lessons.hint: When your mum says she has called you 'one thousand times', is she actually counting, or is she telling you how vexed she is?

lessons.question: A poet describes a daughter's wedding as 'a joyful mourning'. What is the best explanation of this phrase?
options: It is a mistake, because joy and mourning cannot exist together
It is a simile comparing a wedding to a funeral
It is hyperbole exaggerating how sad weddings are
It is an oxymoron capturing the family's mixed feelings
lessons.explanation: An oxymoron puts two opposite words side by side on purpose. Here it captures real mixed emotion: happiness at the wedding and grief that the daughter is leaving home.
lessons.hint: Think of a mother at her daughter's traditional marriage, smiling and crying at the same time. Can two opposite feelings sit in one heart?

lessons.question: In a novel, an elder says 'The crown will decide the matter,' and later a narrator says 'All hands were needed on the farm.' Which is correct?
options: Both are synecdoche because both replace people with objects
Both are personification of objects and body parts
lessons.explanation: A crown is associated with a king but is not part of him, so it is metonymy. Hands are an actual part of the workers, so using a part for the whole is synecdoche.
lessons.hint: Is the item a real PART of the person, like a finger, or just something linked to them, like a cap on Oga's head?

lessons.question: A poem describes a village smithy: 'the hammer's clang rang through the forge.' What device does 'clang' illustrate?
options: Alliteration, because it repeats a consonant
Onomatopoeia, because the word imitates the sound
A random word choice with no special effect
lessons.explanation: 'Clang' sounds like metal striking metal, so it is onomatopoeia. It lets the reader almost hear the forge instead of just being told about it.
lessons.hint: Say the word out loud. Does it sound like the thing it describes, the way 'gbam' sounds like a door slamming?

lessons.question: A poem about captives contains the line 'silent, sullen, suffering slaves'. What is the main effect of the repeated 's' sound?
options: Its hushed, drawn-out sound deepens the mood of heavy oppression
It is only decoration to make the line sound pretty
It makes the line rhyme with the next one
It shows the slaves are happy and singing
lessons.explanation: Alliteration is not just decoration. The slow, hissing 's' sound reinforces the heaviness and suppressed suffering the words describe.
lessons.hint: Read it slowly. Does it sound quick and cheerful like a highlife beat, or slow and heavy like a long sigh?

lessons.question: Consider the line 'the moon swoons over the lagoon'. The repeated 'oo' sound in 'moon', 'swoons' and 'lagoon' is an example of:
options: End-rhyme, since the words sound alike
Onomatopoeia, since the moon makes a sound
Assonance, the repetition of vowel sounds within a line
lessons.explanation: Assonance repeats vowel sounds inside and across words in a line, giving a smooth, musical flow. End-rhyme only happens at the ends of lines, and alliteration repeats consonants.
lessons.hint: Is the repeated sound a vowel or a consonant? And is it only at the end of the line, or spread across it?

lessons.question: In a protest poem, almost every line of the second stanza begins with 'We shall...' ('We shall rise... We shall build... We shall not bow...'). What is the effect?
options: It is a stylistic habit with no real purpose
Anaphora builds momentum and a tone of collective resolve
It shows the poet ran out of new words
It creates a refrain that ends every stanza
lessons.explanation: Repeating the same words at the start of successive lines is anaphora. Each 'We shall' adds weight, building rising determination like a crowd chanting together.
lessons.hint: Picture a rally where the crowd answers each point with the same opening words. Does the energy go up or down?

lessons.question: In a poem about a chase, many lines have no punctuation at the end and run straight into the next: 'He ran through the market and down / the hill and into the night'. Why?
options: It is a printing error in the poem
It is caesura, a pause in the middle of the line
It is enjambment, creating urgency and breathless movement
It is free verse, so the lines have no structure
lessons.explanation: Enjambment lets a sentence spill over a line break without stopping. Here it carries the reader forward without rest, mirroring the breathless chase.
lessons.hint: If you read it aloud, do you get a chance to pause and catch your breath, like a danfo that refuses to stop at the bus stop?

lessons.question: A storyteller begins a folktale by calling 'Story, story!' and the audience replies 'Story!' What is the main function of this opening?
options: It is an opening formula that gains attention and frames the tale
It is meaningless filler before the real story starts
It tells the audience the moral of the story
It is a riddle the audience must solve
lessons.explanation: Opening formulae are conventions that mark entry into the world of the tale. The call-and-reply wins attention and shows the audience agrees to take part.
lessons.hint: Think of how a church service or a school assembly opens with a set greeting. What does that opening do to the crowd?

lessons.question: An oral work song goes: Leader: 'Who will carry the load?' Chorus: 'We will carry it!' This pattern repeats throughout. What is it, and why is it used?
options: Mere repetition that makes the song boring
A refrain that only the leader sings
A dirge that mourns the workers' suffering
Call-and-response, creating communal participation and rhythm
lessons.explanation: One voice calls and the group answers. This call-and-response builds unity, keeps the rhythm of the work, and lets everyone share in the performance.
lessons.hint: Remember a football chant or a 'Gbosa!' reply. Who is talking, one person or everybody?

lessons.question: In a novel, an elder rarely speaks plainly and instead uses proverbs such as 'The lizard that jumps from the tall iroko will praise itself.' Why does the writer make him speak this way?
options: To slow the story down and fill pages
Proverbs carry ancestral authority and persuade wisely and tactfully
Because the elder cannot speak English well
Proverbs are decorations with no role in the argument
lessons.explanation: Proverbs carry the weight of communal wisdom, so they persuade powerfully and can soften criticism. They also mark the elder as wise and respected.
lessons.hint: When your grandfather wants to correct you without shouting, how does he do it? Does a proverb make his point weaker or stronger?

lessons.question: An exam question says: 'Discuss the tortoise as a trickster figure.' Which view best fits the trickster in Nigerian folktales?
options: He is purely evil and the tales want us to hate him
He is a pure hero whose actions are always good
He is admired for his wit but punished for his greed and deceit
He is a minor character with no real importance
lessons.explanation: The trickster is ambivalent: we enjoy his cleverness against stronger animals, yet his greed is often punished, as with his cracked shell. The tales both entertain and warn.
lessons.hint: Think of a very 'sharp guy' in your area. You laugh at his clever stunts, but would you trust him with your money?

lessons.question: An oral poem says of a dead farmer: 'Who will now feed the goats? / Who will wake the compound at cockcrow? / Our pillar has fallen.' What type of oral poem is this?
options: A dirge, lamenting the dead with sorrowful rhetorical questions
A praise poem, because it says good things about him
A folktale, because it tells a story about a farmer
An incantation, because it repeats questions
lessons.explanation: A dirge is a funeral lament. Its sorrowful tone, rhetorical questions about the loss and remembrance of the person's virtues all point to mourning, not simple praise.
lessons.hint: The person in the poem is gone. At what kind of gathering would people ask 'who will now do this for us?'

lessons.question: Right after his shop burns down, a trader looks at the ashes and says, 'What a wonderful day.' What device is the writer using?
options: Dramatic irony, because the audience knows more
Hyperbole, because he exaggerates the day
Situational irony, because the fire was unexpected
Verbal irony, saying the opposite of what he means
lessons.explanation: He says 'wonderful' but means terrible, which is verbal irony. It shows his devastation hidden behind bitter humour.
lessons.hint: Focus on his WORDS. Does what he says match what he truly feels, like when someone stuck in Lagos traffic says 'I'm enjoying myself'?

lessons.question: A man builds a high fence to keep thieves away from his house, but it turns out that the thief is his own son. Why is this situational irony and not just a plot twist?
options: Because any surprising event in a story is irony
Because the outcome directly contradicts what his effort was meant to achieve
Because the son says the opposite of what he means
Because the audience knew about the son from the start
lessons.explanation: Situational irony is a specific gap between what is expected or intended and what happens. The fence was built against thieves, yet the thief was inside all along.
lessons.hint: A twist is any surprise. Ask: does the ending turn the man's own plan upside down?

lessons.question: In a play, the audience has seen conspirators plan a night attack. Later the watchman tells the villagers, 'Nothing bad will happen tonight.' What does this create?
options: A coincidence in the plot with no special effect
Verbal irony, because the watchman is being sarcastic
Dramatic irony, building tension because we know more than he does
Comic relief, because the watchman is a minor character
lessons.explanation: Dramatic irony happens when the audience knows something a character does not. His confident words fill us with dread because we know the attack is coming.
lessons.hint: Who in the hall knows about the plan: the watchman, or you sitting in the audience?

lessons.question: A question asks you to 'examine the playwright's use of satire'. Which statement best explains how satire relates to irony?
options: Satire is a mode that ridicules vice; irony is one of its tools
Satire and irony are exactly the same thing
Irony is the purpose; satire is a small technique inside it
Satire is only found in poems, irony only in plays
lessons.explanation: Satire is the overall purpose of exposing and mocking folly or corruption, often to push for change. Irony, exaggeration and caricature are some of the tools it uses.
lessons.hint: Think of a comedy skit mocking politicians. The aim is to criticise; what tricks does the comedian use to do it?

lessons.question: In a play, a clever old woman asks a corrupt councillor: 'Please, my son, where did the road money go? I'm just an old woman, I don't understand these things.' What is she doing?
options: Showing genuine confusion about government money
Using hyperbole about her age and weakness
Showing respect by calling him 'my son'
Using feigned ignorance (Socratic irony) to expose his corruption
lessons.explanation: She pretends to be simple so her innocent-looking questions force the councillor to reveal his guilt in public. Her 'ignorance' actually shows how sharp she is.
lessons.hint: Have you seen an elder 'play dumb' to catch someone in a lie? Is she really confused, or is she setting a trap?

lessons.question: In a play, a character stands alone on stage and speaks his secret fears and plans aloud for a long time. What is this convention called, and why is it used?
options: A dialogue, to show his relationship with other characters
A soliloquy, to reveal his inner thoughts directly to the audience
An aside, to make a quick joke to another character
Exposition, to give background on the setting
lessons.explanation: A soliloquy is spoken by a character alone on stage, letting the audience hear his private thoughts. It is a stage convention, not meant to be realistic.
lessons.hint: He is alone, and nobody else on stage hears him. So who is he really talking to?

lessons.question: During a family meeting on stage, a character mutters, 'If only they knew what I did,' and the text shows the other characters do not react at all. What is this?
options: An aside, heard by the audience but not by the other characters
A mistake by the playwright, since others should hear him
A soliloquy, since only one character is speaking
A monologue addressed to the whole family
lessons.explanation: An aside is a short remark the audience hears but the other characters, by convention, do not. It reveals a private reaction in the middle of the action.
lessons.hint: Others are present on stage this time, yet they don't react. It's like whispering to your friend in the back row during assembly.

lessons.question: In the middle of a tense scene where a chief is accused of murder, two drunk palace guards argue comically over a stolen chicken. What is the playwright's purpose?
options: To ruin the serious mood the play has built
To show the playwright could not maintain the tension
To provide comic relief, giving the audience a breather
To introduce the main conflict of the play
lessons.explanation: Comic relief gives the audience a short emotional rest without erasing the seriousness. It can even make the tragedy hit harder when the tension returns.
lessons.hint: During a long, stressful exam period, why do students still crack jokes in the hostel? What does a little laughter do?

lessons.question: Early in Act One, a stage direction reads: '(He fingers a small dagger hidden in his sleeve.)' Nothing happens with the dagger until much later. Why include it?
options: It is filler that has no importance
It is exposition about the character's family background
It is comic relief to lighten the mood
It is foreshadowing, hinting at violence to come
lessons.explanation: Foreshadowing plants an early hint that becomes important later. The hidden dagger prepares the attentive audience for danger ahead.
lessons.hint: In a Nollywood film, when the camera lingers on a gun in a drawer, do you expect it to stay in the drawer forever?

lessons.question: In a tragedy, a proud king loses his throne and wealth; soon after, he discovers that his own decree caused his son's death. Which term matches the DISCOVERY?
options: Anagnorisis, the character's recognition moving from ignorance to knowledge
Catharsis, the audience's release of pity and fear
Comic relief, the audience's emotional breather
lessons.explanation: Peripeteia is the reversal of fortune (losing the throne), while anagnorisis is the moment of recognition (discovering the truth). They often come close together but are different.
lessons.hint: Separate what HAPPENS to him (the fall) from what he finally KNOWS (the truth). Which one is the question asking about?

lessons.question: An unseen poem begins: 'I sold my mother's wrapper to buy a lottery ticket.' The question asks you to describe 'the speaker'. Who is the speaker?
options: The poet, confessing what he did in real life
The reader, whom the poem is accusing
A persona, a voice the poet creates, such as a desperate gambler
The mother, whose wrapper was sold
lessons.explanation: The 'I' in a poem is a speaker or persona created by the poet, not necessarily the poet himself. Here the persona lets the poet explore and criticise gambling.
lessons.hint: When a Nollywood actor plays a thief, is he confessing his own life? Who is the 'I' in a poem really?

lessons.question: A question asks for both the tone and the mood of a flood poem. Which pair of definitions is correct?
options: Tone and mood mean the same thing, so one word answers both
Tone is the poem's subject; mood is its rhyme scheme
Tone is the reader's feeling; mood is the poet's attitude
Tone is the speaker's attitude; mood is the atmosphere felt by the reader
lessons.explanation: Tone is the speaker's attitude to the subject, shown through word choice (for example, bitter). Mood is the atmosphere the poem creates in the reader (for example, gloomy).
lessons.hint: Think of a teacher announcing results. Her voice may sound calm (her attitude), but the class still feels tense (the atmosphere). Which is which?

lessons.question: A poem's first two stanzas describe wedding drums and dancing. Stanza three begins: 'Yet the mother's eyes search for the son who is not here.' What is the best comment on tone?
options: The tone is joyful throughout, because of the wedding
The tone shifts at 'Yet' from celebration to sorrow
The tone is angry, because the son refused to come
The tone is neutral, since it only describes events
lessons.explanation: The word 'Yet' signals a turn. The joyful opening makes the mother's grief for her absent son more painful by contrast, so tone must be tracked across the poem.
lessons.hint: Watch out for little turning words like 'but', 'yet' and 'however'. They are like a driver's indicator: a change of direction is coming.

lessons.question: A sonnet has three quatrains (ABAB CDCD EFEF) praising a harmattan morning, then ends with a rhyming couplet (GG) about a homeless man shivering in its cold. What does the couplet do?
options: It concludes with a twist that undercuts the earlier praise
It simply repeats what the quatrains already said
It has no special role; it is just the last two lines
It introduces a refrain that will repeat later
lessons.explanation: In a Shakespearean sonnet the final couplet often summarises or twists the argument. Here it turns the praise around by revealing the harmattan's harsh side.
lessons.hint: At the end of a long speech, what does a good speaker save for the last line: something forgettable, or the punchline?

lessons.question: In a poem, a landlord tells a silent new tenant how generous he is, adding that he evicted the last tenant 'only because the man was ungrateful' for a rent increase. What does the poem reveal?
options: The landlord is truly generous and kind
The tenant is ungrateful and dishonest
The poet personally dislikes all landlords
In this dramatic monologue, the landlord unknowingly exposes his own greed
lessons.explanation: In a dramatic monologue, one speaker addresses a silent listener and reveals more than he intends. His own details contradict his claims of generosity, creating irony.
lessons.hint: Don't just believe what he says about himself. Look at what he actually DID. Does his story match his self-praise?

lessons.question: A danfo bus travelling at 20 m/s brakes and comes to rest in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
lessons.explanation: a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 20)/4 = -5 m/s^2. The negative sign shows deceleration.
lessons.hint: 'Comes to rest' tells you the final velocity. Which one is it when the bus stops at the bus stop?

lessons.question: Two danfo buses move toward each other on a straight road, one at 15 m/s and the other at 10 m/s. At what speed are they approaching each other?
lessons.explanation: Moving in opposite directions, the speeds add: 15 + 10 = 25 m/s.
lessons.hint: If you and your friend walk toward each other in a market, does the gap close faster or slower than if only one of you moved?

lessons.question: A stone is dropped from the top of a water tower and hits the ground after 3 s. Taking g = 10 m/s^2 and ignoring air resistance, how tall is the tower?
lessons.hint: 'Dropped' tells you the starting speed, like a mango falling straight off the branch. Which term disappears?

lessons.question: An okada rider increases speed from 4 m/s to 12 m/s while covering 32 m. What is the acceleration?
lessons.explanation: No time is given, so use v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s: 144 = 16 + 64*a, so a = 128/64 = 2 m/s^2.
lessons.hint: You know u, v and s but not t. Pick the equation of motion that has no t in it.

lessons.question: A boy throws a stone horizontally at 20 m/s from the top of a 45 m cliff. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, how long does it take to hit the ground?
lessons.explanation: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal speed: t = sqrt(2*h/g) = sqrt(2*45/10) = sqrt(9) = 3 s.
lessons.hint: Does throwing a stone sideways make gravity pull it down any faster or slower? Focus only on the vertical drop.

lessons.question: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. What is its speed?
lessons.hint: Each second, 50 waves pass and each is 4 m long, like 50 danfos of 4 m each driving past you. How much road is covered?

lessons.question: A talking drum's skin completes 4 oscillations in 2 s. What is the period of the oscillation?
lessons.explanation: T = time/number of oscillations = 2/4 = 0.5 s (the frequency is 4/2 = 2 Hz, and T = 1/f).
lessons.hint: Period is the time for ONE oscillation. If 4 happen in 2 s, how long does each one take?

lessons.question: A boy shouts toward a rock face at Olumo Rock and hears the echo 2 s later. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, how far away is the rock face?
lessons.explanation: The 2 s is a round trip, so one-way time = 1 s: distance = 340*1 = 340 m.
lessons.hint: The sound has to travel to the rock AND come back, like going to the market and returning home. How much of the time is one way?

lessons.question: An open pipe (open at both ends) of length 0.34 m is sounding its fundamental note. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the fundamental frequency?
lessons.explanation: For an open pipe λ = 2*L = 0.68 m, so f = v/λ = 340/0.68 = 500 Hz.
lessons.hint: An open pipe like a flute has an antinode at both ends. How many quarter-wavelengths fit between two antinodes with one node in the middle?

lessons.question: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.5 m. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is its fundamental (lowest) frequency?
lessons.explanation: For a closed pipe λ = 4*L = 4*0.5 = 2 m, so f = v/λ = 340/2 = 170 Hz.
lessons.hint: Blowing across an empty Coke bottle: the closed bottom is a node and the open mouth an antinode. What fraction of a wavelength is that?

lessons.question: A bulb in a rechargeable lantern has 12 V across it and a current of 3 A flowing through it. What is its resistance?
lessons.hint: Ohm's law is V = I*R. Which quantity do you divide by which to leave R alone?

lessons.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
lessons.explanation: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 12/5 = 2.4 Ω, smaller than either resistor.
lessons.hint: Opening a second gate at a crowded stadium makes it easier for people to leave. Should the combined resistance be bigger or smaller than 4 Ω?

lessons.question: A 2 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors. What is the total resistance?
lessons.explanation: Parallel part: 1/R = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. Total = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω.
lessons.hint: Simplify the parallel pair first, like sorting out the side-road before joining the main expressway.

lessons.question: A keke battery has an e.m.f. of 12 V and an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω. What is its terminal voltage when it delivers a current of 2 A?
lessons.explanation: V = E - I*r = 12 - 2*0.5 = 11 V; 1 V is 'lost' inside the battery.
lessons.hint: Some of the battery's voltage is used up pushing current through its own insides. Should the terminal voltage be more or less than 12 V?

lessons.question: A 1500 W pressing iron is used for 2 hours every day for 30 days. If one unit (1 kWh) costs ₦70, what is the total cost?
lessons.hint: NEPA bills in kWh, not Wh. Convert the iron's power to kilowatts before you multiply.

lessons.question: A windlass over a village well has a handle that turns in a circle of radius 40 cm. The axle the rope winds on has radius 8 cm. What is the velocity ratio?
lessons.hint: In one turn, your hand travels round the big circle while the rope winds round the small axle. Compare the two circles.

lessons.question: A wheelbarrow carries a 600 N load of sand whose weight acts 0.4 m from the wheel axle. The handles are 1.2 m from the axle. What upward effort is needed at the handles?
lessons.explanation: Moments about the axle: E*1.2 = 600*0.4 = 240, so E = 240/1.2 = 200 N.
lessons.hint: The wheel is the pivot. Measure both distances from the axle, then balance the moments.

lessons.question: A pulley system with velocity ratio 4 lifts an 800 N load at a building site with an effort of 250 N. What is its efficiency?
lessons.hint: First find MA from load and effort. A real machine on a site can never beat 100%, so check your answer.

lessons.question: A labourer lifts a 500 N bag of cement through 2 m using a pulley. He pulls with a force of 200 N and draws in 6 m of rope. What is the efficiency?
lessons.hint: Efficiency = useful work out / work put in. Which work does the cement get, and which does the labourer do?

lessons.question: A machine has a velocity ratio of 5 and an efficiency of 70%. What effort is needed to lift a load of 1400 N?
lessons.hint: Use efficiency and VR to find MA first. Friction means you need MORE effort than an ideal machine would.

units.title: Mama Put Kitchen: Heat and Gases

lessons.question: How much heat is needed to completely melt 0.2 kg of ice at 0°C? (Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336000 J/kg)
lessons.explanation: Melting happens at constant temperature, so Q = m*L = 0.2*336000 = 67200 J (no Δθ term).
lessons.hint: Ice in your pure water sachet melts without its temperature changing. Which formula has no Δθ in it?

lessons.question: How much heat is needed to raise 0.5 kg of water in a kettle from 25°C to 100°C? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg*K))
lessons.hint: Use the CHANGE in temperature, not the final reading. How many degrees does the water actually rise?

lessons.question: A 2 kg block of iron absorbs 45000 J of heat and its temperature rises from 20°C to 70°C. What is the specific heat capacity of iron?
lessons.hint: Specific heat capacity is heat per kilogram per degree. Make sure both the mass and the temperature rise are in your denominator.

lessons.question: A fixed mass of gas in a bicycle pump is at 100 kPa and occupies 6 L. It is compressed to 3 L at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
lessons.explanation: Boyle's law: P_1*V_1 = P_2*V_2, so 100*6 = P_2*3 and P_2 = 200 kPa.
lessons.hint: Squeeze the same air into half the space, like passengers packed into a smaller bus. Do they hit the walls more or less often?

lessons.question: A gas occupies 300 cm^3 at 27°C. What is its volume at 127°C if the pressure stays constant?
lessons.hint: Gas laws only work with temperature measured from absolute zero. Convert both Celsius readings first.

lessons.question: A capacitor stores a charge of 60 μC when connected across a 12 V battery. What is its capacitance?
lessons.explanation: C = Q/V = 60 μC/12 V = 5 μF, i.e. 5 μC stored per volt.
lessons.hint: Capacitance is charge stored PER volt, a bit like price per litre at the filling station. Divide or multiply?

lessons.question: A charge of 5*10^-6 C placed in an electric field experiences a force of 0.02 N. What is the electric field intensity?
lessons.hint: Field strength is force per unit charge. Divide the force by the charge, and watch the power of ten.

lessons.question: The electrostatic force between two point charges is 0.8 N. If the distance between them is halved, what is the new force?
lessons.explanation: F ∝ 1/r^2, so halving r multiplies F by 2^2 = 4: F = 4*0.8 = 3.2 N.
lessons.hint: Coulomb's law has r squared at the bottom. What happens to 1/r^2 when r becomes r/2?

lessons.question: Two point charges of 2 μC and 3 μC are 0.3 m apart in air. What is the force between them? (k = 9*10^9 N m^2/C^2)
lessons.hint: Convert μC to C (1 μC = 10^-6 C) and remember to square the distance.

lessons.question: A 2 μF and a 4 μF capacitor are in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 3 μF capacitor. The network is connected across 12 V. What charge flows from the battery?
lessons.explanation: Parallel: 2 + 4 = 6 μF; series with 3 μF: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF. Q = C*V = 2*12 = 24 μC.
lessons.hint: Capacitors follow the opposite rules to resistors: add in parallel, reciprocals in series. Reduce the parallel pair first.

lessons.question: Mama Ngozi buys goods for resale worth ₦5,000 and pays cash immediately. Which entry records this in her books?
lessons.explanation: Goods coming in are debited to Purchases; cash going out is credited to Cash. Debit the receiver, credit the giver.
lessons.hint: When you buy pure water with cash, the sachets come in and the naira leaves your pocket. Which account receives, which one gives?

lessons.question: A business sells goods on credit to Chidi for ₦8,000. Which entry is correct?
lessons.explanation: Chidi now owes the business ₦8,000, so his account is debited; Sales is credited because goods went out as revenue.
lessons.hint: No cash changed hands, so who now 'owes' the shop, like a customer who says 'I go pay you next week'?

lessons.question: The owner of a provisions shop takes goods costing ₦4,000 home for his family's use. No cash is paid. How is this recorded?
lessons.explanation: Goods taken by the owner are drawings (debit Drawings) and they reduce goods bought for resale (credit Purchases). No cash moved, so Cash is not touched.
lessons.hint: If you take Indomie from your own shop for dinner, the shop did not 'spend' money. You took the value out. Which account tracks what the owner takes?

lessons.question: A debtor who owed ₦10,000 pays ₦9,500 cash in full settlement, and is allowed a discount of ₦500. With what amount is the debtor's account credited?
lessons.explanation: Cash ₦9,500 plus Discount Allowed ₦500 are both debited, so the debtor is credited with the full ₦10,000 to clear the debt.
lessons.hint: The customer's slate must go to zero. How much did he owe before you 'dashed' him the discount?

lessons.question: A trader sells goods for ₦22,000, a figure that already includes 10% VAT. What amount should be credited to the Sales account?
lessons.explanation: Net sales = ₦22,000 / 1.10 = ₦20,000. The ₦2,000 VAT is owed to the tax authority, so it is a liability, not revenue.
lessons.hint: VAT is like money a friend asks you to hold for someone else. It passes through your hand but it is not yours. Is the 10% on the net price or on the total?

lessons.question: A business has total assets of ₦300,000 and total liabilities of ₦120,000. What is the owner's capital?
lessons.explanation: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = ₦300,000 − ₦120,000 = ₦180,000.
lessons.hint: If your shop goods are worth plenty but you still owe the wholesaler, what is truly yours after you settle him?

lessons.question: Sales ₦200,000; opening stock ₦30,000; purchases ₦120,000; closing stock ₦25,000. What is the gross profit?
lessons.hint: Goods left on your shelf at year end were not sold. Should their cost be part of what you 'used up' to make sales?

lessons.question: Gross profit is ₦75,000. Rent is ₦10,000, wages are ₦20,000, and discount received is ₦5,000. What is the net profit?
lessons.explanation: Discount received is income, so it is added: ₦75,000 + ₦5,000 − ₦10,000 − ₦20,000 = ₦50,000.
lessons.hint: When the wholesaler at Balogun market knocks something off your bill, did you gain or lose?

lessons.question: Debtors at year end total ₦80,000. A 5% provision for doubtful debts is created. What figure for debtors appears in the balance sheet (net)?
lessons.explanation: Provision = 5% × ₦80,000 = ₦4,000; it is deducted from debtors, giving ₦76,000 (prudence concept).
lessons.hint: If you suspect some customers who buy on credit will never pay, do you show the full amount they owe or a more careful figure?

lessons.question: Sales ₦500,000; opening stock ₦40,000; purchases ₦280,000; closing stock ₦60,000; total expenses ₦90,000. What is the net profit?
lessons.hint: Do it in two steps like climbing stairs: find gross profit first, then remove the running expenses.

lessons.question: A machine cost ₦100,000, has a scrap value of ₦10,000 and a useful life of 5 years. What is the annual depreciation using the straight line method?
lessons.explanation: (Cost − Scrap value) / Life = (₦100,000 − ₦10,000) / 5 = ₦18,000 per year.
lessons.hint: If you can still sell the old machine to a scrap buyer at the end, should that part of the cost be 'used up' over the years?

lessons.question: A machine costing ₦120,000 is bought exactly halfway through the financial year. Depreciation is 10% per annum, straight line, time-apportioned. What is this year's charge?
lessons.explanation: Full year = 10% × ₦120,000 = ₦12,000; owned for half the year, so ₦12,000 × 1/2 = ₦6,000.
lessons.hint: If you rent a shop for only six months, do you pay the whole year's rent? How long was this machine actually used this year?

lessons.question: A vehicle cost ₦500,000 and is depreciated at 20% per annum on the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation for the SECOND year?
lessons.hint: Like a danfo bus that loses value each year, reducing balance applies the rate to what is LEFT, not to the original price.

lessons.question: A generator costs ₦200,000 and is depreciated at 25% per annum on the reducing balance method. What is its net book value at the end of 2 years?
lessons.hint: Your 'I better pass my neighbour' generator loses a quarter of its remaining value each year. Work year by year, not from the shop price each time.

lessons.question: A machine that cost ₦75,000, with accumulated depreciation of ₦30,000, is sold for ₦60,000. How is the result treated?
options: Sales revenue of ₦60,000 in trading account
Loss on disposal of ₦15,000 in P&L
Profit on disposal of ₦30,000 in P&L
Profit on disposal of ₦15,000 in P&L
lessons.explanation: NBV = ₦75,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦45,000; proceeds ₦60,000 exceed NBV by ₦15,000, a profit on disposal shown as other income, not sales.
lessons.hint: Selling your old okada is not your normal trade. Compare the cash you got with what the okada was worth in your books.

lessons.question: The bank statement shows a bank charge of ₦500 that has not been entered in the cash book. What should be done?
options: Deduct ₦500 from the cash book balance
Add ₦500 to the cash book balance
Add ₦500 to the bank statement balance
No entry; it is only a timing difference
lessons.explanation: The bank has already recorded its own charge correctly, so the cash book is updated: the ₦500 is credited (deducted) in the cash book.
lessons.hint: When you get a debit alert for SMS charges, who needs to update their records: the bank, or you?

lessons.question: A trader paid ₦15,000 into the bank on the last day of the month, but it is not yet on the bank statement. How is it treated in the bank reconciliation statement?
options: Deduct ₦15,000 from the bank statement balance
Deduct ₦15,000 from the cash book balance
Add ₦15,000 to the bank statement balance
Add ₦15,000 to the cash book balance
lessons.explanation: This is an uncredited lodgement: the cash book already shows it, so ₦15,000 is added to the bank statement balance to reconcile.
lessons.hint: Money you sent that 'has not dropped' yet is still yours. Which record is missing it, your book or the bank's?

lessons.question: The bank statement shows ₦52,000. A cheque of ₦7,000 issued to a supplier has not yet been presented. What is the adjusted bank statement balance?
lessons.explanation: Adjusted balance = ₦52,000 − ₦7,000 = ₦45,000; the unpresented cheque is already deducted in the cash book.
lessons.hint: The supplier has not gone to cash the cheque yet, but the money is already promised. Should it still count as available?

lessons.question: A customer's cheque for ₦18,000, already recorded as received and banked, is returned dishonoured. Which entry corrects the books?
lessons.explanation: The original receipt is reversed: Bank is credited because the money never arrived, and the customer is debited because he still owes.
lessons.hint: If someone's transfer is reversed, have they paid you? Undo the original entry.

lessons.question: A bank statement shows ₦102,000. There are unpresented cheques of ₦30,000 and an uncredited lodgement of ₦13,000. What is the adjusted bank statement balance?
lessons.hint: Cheques you wrote will soon leave the account; money you paid in will soon arrive. Which way does each one move the bank's figure?

lessons.question: Musa (capital ₦300,000) and Tunde (capital ₦100,000) run a provisions shop with no partnership agreement. Net profit is ₦80,000. What is Musa's share?
lessons.explanation: With no agreement, the Partnership Act rule is that profits are shared equally, so Musa gets ₦80,000 / 2 = ₦40,000.
lessons.hint: If two brothers never agreed on sharing, what does the law say: share by money contributed, or share alike?

lessons.question: Chidi and Emeka share profits in the ratio 3:2. Residual profit after salaries and interest on capital is ₦100,000. What is Chidi's share?
lessons.hint: Sharing suya 3:2 means cutting it into how many equal pieces first?

lessons.question: Funke and Grace admit Halima as a partner. Halima pays ₦150,000 cash into the business bank account as her capital. Which entry is correct?
options: Debit Bank, Credit Halima's Current Account
Debit Bank, Credit Funke's and Grace's Capital
lessons.explanation: Bank receives ₦150,000 (debit), and Halima's Capital account is credited with her long-term stake in the business.
lessons.hint: Think of joining an esusu group: your contribution goes into the pot, and the group records it under YOUR name. Which type of account holds a partner's fixed investment?

lessons.question: Ibrahim's current account opens with a credit balance of ₦15,000. He is credited with salary ₦30,000, interest on capital ₦8,000 and profit share ₦42,000. His drawings are ₦50,000. What is the closing balance?
lessons.explanation: Credits ₦95,000 less drawings ₦50,000 = ₦45,000 credit balance owed to Ibrahim.
lessons.hint: Salary and profit share are what the business 'owes' him; drawings are what he has already collected. Which side does each go?

lessons.question: Ade and Bola share profits equally. Net profit is ₦200,000. Ade gets a salary of ₦40,000. Interest on capital: Ade ₦20,000, Bola ₦10,000. What is Ade's total share?
lessons.hint: Like sharing a party's leftover jollof: serve the agreed special portions first, then split what remains.

lessons.question: A club's accumulated fund at the start of the year is ₦180,000. The income and expenditure account shows a DEFICIT of ₦22,000. What is the closing accumulated fund?
lessons.explanation: A deficit reduces the accumulated fund: ₦180,000 − ₦22,000 = ₦158,000. Only a surplus is added.
lessons.hint: If your town union spent more than it earned this year, does its savings pot grow or shrink?

lessons.question: A town union starts the year with cash of ₦45,000. Receipts: levies ₦120,000, donations ₦30,000, bazaar ₦55,000. Payments: hall rent ₦60,000, refreshments ₦25,000, plastic chairs ₦80,000. What is the closing cash balance?
lessons.explanation: Closing cash = ₦45,000 + ₦205,000 − ₦165,000 = ₦85,000. All cash paid, including chairs, appears in receipts and payments.
lessons.hint: Count the cash box like a treasurer: what was inside before the year started? Then every naira in and out, including the chairs.

lessons.question: A club paid rent of ₦40,000 this year, including ₦8,000 owed from last year. At year end ₦6,000 rent is still owing. What rent goes into the income and expenditure account?
lessons.explanation: Rent expense = ₦40,000 − ₦8,000 (last year's) + ₦6,000 (still owing) = ₦38,000.
lessons.hint: Last year's debt to the landlord belongs to last year. This year's unpaid rent is still this year's cost.

lessons.question: An old students' association received ₦80,000 dues in 2024: ₦5,000 was for 2023 and ₦3,000 was for 2025. Members still owe ₦7,000 for 2024. What is the 2024 subscription income?
lessons.explanation: ₦80,000 − ₦5,000 − ₦3,000 + ₦7,000 = ₦79,000. Only dues that belong to 2024 count, paid or not.
lessons.hint: Ask of each naira: 'Is this dues FOR 2024?' Not 'Did it ENTER the purse in 2024?'

lessons.question: Subscriptions: arrears at 1 Jan ₦4,000; in advance at 1 Jan ₦2,500; cash received ₦96,000; arrears at 31 Dec ₦6,000; in advance at 31 Dec ₦3,500. What subscription income goes to the income and expenditure account?
lessons.hint: Opening arrears were already counted as last year's income; opening advance was paid last year for THIS year. Which one adds, which one subtracts?

lessons.question: In the sentence 'Ada walked quickly to the market', what part of speech is the word 'quickly'?
lessons.explanation: 'Quickly' tells us how Ada walked, so it describes the verb 'walked'. Words that describe verbs are adverbs.
lessons.hint: Ask yourself: is 'quickly' describing a person or thing, or describing an action?

lessons.question: Choose the correct word to fill the gap: Each of the boys ______ a cutlass for Labour Day.
lessons.explanation: 'Each' is the real subject and it is singular, so it takes a singular verb. 'Of the boys' does not change that.
lessons.hint: Find the real subject. Is it 'boys', or the word before 'of'?

lessons.question: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to the underlined word: Alhaji is very GENEROUS to the poor in his street.
lessons.explanation: A generous person gives freely. The opposite is someone who does not like to give or share at all.
lessons.hint: Opposite, not similar. Which word describes someone who hates to share?

lessons.question: Choose the correct option: By the time NEPA restored the light, we ______ our homework.
lessons.explanation: Two actions happened in the past, and the homework was done first. The earlier past action uses the past perfect tense.
lessons.hint: 'Restored' is already in the past. Did the homework end before or after that?

lessons.question: Which of these sentences is correctly punctuated?
options: Tundes' mother sells rice, beans and garri.
Tunde's mother sells, rice beans and garri.
Tunde's mother sells rice, beans and garri.
Tundes mother sells rice beans, and garri.
lessons.explanation: One person (Tunde) owns 'mother', so we write Tunde's. Commas separate items in a list, not the verb from its object.
lessons.hint: Check two things: the apostrophe for ONE owner, and where the list of foodstuff begins.

lessons.question: A block of ice left on a table at the market turns into water. What is this change called?
lessons.explanation: Ice is a solid and water is a liquid. A change from solid to liquid caused by heat is called melting.
lessons.hint: Which state does the ice start in, and which state does it end in?

lessons.question: A torchlight battery stores energy before it is used. In what form is the energy stored in the battery?
lessons.explanation: A battery contains chemicals that react to produce electricity. So the energy is stored as chemical energy until the torch is switched on.
lessons.hint: The light only appears when you switch on. What is inside the battery before then?

lessons.question: Which part of the blood helps the body to fight germs and diseases?
lessons.explanation: White blood cells attack and destroy germs, so they defend the body against infection.
lessons.hint: Think of the jobs: carrying oxygen, clotting, carrying food, and fighting germs.

lessons.question: In a wheelbarrow, the wheel is the fulcrum and the load sits between the wheel and the handles. What class of lever is a wheelbarrow?
lessons.explanation: When the load is between the fulcrum and the effort, the lever is a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow or nutcracker.
lessons.hint: Find what is in the MIDDLE: the fulcrum, the load or the effort?

lessons.question: Emeka pushes a cart of yams with a force of 50 N and moves it 6 m along the road. How much work does he do?
lessons.explanation: Work done = force x distance = 50 N x 6 m = 300 J.
lessons.hint: Work needs both the force and the distance. Should you add, subtract, divide or multiply them?

lessons.question: The school secretary needs 200 copies of a printed timetable quickly. Which office machine should she use?
lessons.explanation: A photocopier makes many copies of a document quickly. A stapler joins papers, a perforator punches holes, and a franking machine stamps letters.
lessons.hint: Which machine makes copies, not holes or stamps?

lessons.question: A trader buys tomatoes in Kano and sells them in Lagos. What type of trade is this?
lessons.explanation: Kano and Lagos are both in Nigeria, so buying and selling between them is home (domestic) trade.
lessons.hint: Did the tomatoes ever leave Nigeria?

lessons.question: Mama Bisi bought tinned tomatoes that had expired, and her family fell sick after eating them. Which consumer right was mainly violated?
lessons.explanation: Consumers have the right to be protected from goods that can harm their health. Selling expired food breaks that right.
lessons.hint: What happened to the family's health? Which right protects that?

lessons.question: In a cash book, on which side is money RECEIVED by the business recorded?
lessons.explanation: The rule is 'debit what comes in, credit what goes out'. Cash received comes in, so it goes on the debit (left) side.
lessons.hint: Remember the rule: what comes in goes on one side, what goes out on the other.

lessons.question: Chidi's shop started the day with ₦5,000 cash. He received ₦3,500 from sales and paid ₦2,000 for transport. What is his cash balance at the end of the day?
lessons.explanation: Balance = opening cash + money received - money paid = 5,000 + 3,500 - 2,000 = ₦6,500.
lessons.hint: Add what came in, then take away what went out.

units.title: Mama Put Maths: Count Your Change

lessons.question: What is the value of the digit 7 in the number 47,385?
lessons.explanation: Counting from the right: 5 is units, 8 is tens, 3 is hundreds, and 7 is thousands. So 7 stands for 7 thousands.
lessons.hint: Start from the right and name each place: units, tens, hundreds...

lessons.question: Ada bought 12 puff-puff. She ate 1/4 of them. How many puff-puff did Ada eat?
lessons.explanation: 1/4 means share into 4 equal groups and take one group. 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
lessons.hint: A quarter means sharing into 4 equal parts.

lessons.question: A school bag costs ₦2,000. The seller gives a 10% discount. How much will you pay now?
lessons.explanation: 10% of ₦2,000 is ₦200. A discount means you pay less: ₦2,000 − ₦200 = ₦1,800.
lessons.hint: First find 10% of the price, then think: does a discount make it cheaper or dearer?

lessons.question: What is the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 4 and 6?
lessons.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12... Multiples of 6: 6, 12... The smallest number in both lists is 12.
lessons.hint: Write out the times table of each number and look for the first number they share.

lessons.question: A rectangular school garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. What is its area?
lessons.explanation: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 m².
lessons.hint: Area is the space inside, not the distance around the edge.

lessons.question: What is the plural of the word 'child'?
lessons.explanation: 'Child' is an irregular noun. We do not add -s; its plural is 'children'.
lessons.hint: Some words don't just take -s. Think of how your teacher calls the whole class.

lessons.question: Choose the word that is OPPOSITE in meaning to 'generous'.
lessons.explanation: A generous person likes to share. The opposite is a person who does not like to share, who is stingy.
lessons.hint: First remember what a generous person does, then find the word for someone who does the reverse.

lessons.question: Fill in the gap: Yesterday, Tunde ______ to the market with his mother.
lessons.explanation: 'Yesterday' shows the action is in the past, so we use the simple past tense 'went'.
lessons.hint: Look at the first word of the sentence. Is it talking about now, or the past?

lessons.question: Which of these words is spelt correctly?
lessons.explanation: The correct spelling is 'receive'. The rule is 'i before e, except after c'.
lessons.hint: Remember the spelling rhyme about 'i' and 'e' after the letter 'c'.

lessons.question: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
lessons.explanation: A sentence starts with a capital letter, a question ends with a question mark, and the bag belongs to Emeka, so we write Emeka's.
lessons.hint: Check three things: the first letter, the mark at the end, and how we show the bag belongs to Emeka.

lessons.question: Which of these is a NON-LIVING thing?
lessons.explanation: Living things grow, feed, breathe and reproduce. A stone does none of these, so it is non-living.
lessons.hint: Ask yourself: which one does not eat, grow or have young ones?

lessons.question: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
lessons.explanation: The root grows under the soil and absorbs water and mineral salts for the plant.
lessons.hint: Water is in the soil. Which part of the plant lives under the soil?

lessons.question: When is the MOST important time to wash your hands with soap and water?
lessons.explanation: Germs on dirty hands can enter the mouth with food. Washing hands before eating helps stop diseases like diarrhoea.
lessons.hint: Germs cause sickness when they get into your mouth. When do your hands go near your mouth most?

lessons.question: Bisi put a cup of water in the freezer. It turned into ice. What is this change called?
lessons.explanation: When liquid water becomes cold enough to turn into solid ice, the change is called freezing.
lessons.hint: Water changed from liquid to solid. Which word describes getting cold enough to become solid?

lessons.question: A see-saw in the school playground is an example of which simple machine?
lessons.explanation: A see-saw is a lever: a stiff bar that turns on a pivot (fulcrum) in the middle.
lessons.hint: Think about the point in the middle that the see-saw turns on.

lit-0079: Think of two ways a village elder might praise a strong young man: 'He fights like a lion' versus 'He is a lion in battle.' Do both sentences use the exact same wording structure, or is there a small but noticeable difference in how directly each one states the comparison?

Exactly the structural difference. Given that one explicitly signals the comparison with a word like 'like' or 'as', while the other states the comparison directly as if it were literally true, which one would you call a simile, and which a metaphor?
lit-0001: Good question. Before I tell you — think about when your mother says 'this yam is stubborn, it refuses to get soft.' Can a yam actually refuse anything?
Exactly that idea. So if the yam can't really 'refuse', what is the writer doing when they say the sun 'refused' to rise?
That's it — that's called personification. Now, why might a poet choose to say the sun 'refused' rather than simply 'the sun did not rise'? What mood does 'refused' add?
lit-0015: When your aunty says 'I have warned you a thousand times not to play near that gutter', has she actually counted a thousand warnings, or is she making a point some other way?

Exactly — she's exaggerating on purpose for effect, not stating a fact. So back in the play, is 'a million times' meant to be counted literally, or is it doing the same job as your aunty's 'a thousand times'?
Right — what's the specific literary term for deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis rather than literal truth, and what emotion is it emphasising here?
lit-0034: Think of a naming ceremony where the grandmother is dancing and singing with the guests, but also quietly weeping because the baby is named after her late husband. Can real feelings actually be that mixed, joy and grief together, in the same moment?

Good. So when a poet deliberately puts two opposite words side by side — 'joyful' and 'mourning' — is that a mistake, or a compressed way of capturing exactly that kind of real, contradictory emotion?

Right — what is the specific term for a figure of speech that combines two contradictory terms for effect, and what mixed emotional truth about the wedding might it be pointing to here — perhaps a bride leaving her family home?
lit-0111: Let's look closely at the relationship in each case. Is a 'crown' literally a PART of the king's body, the way a 'hand' is literally a PART of a worker's body?

No wahala, let's narrow it down: when you substitute something CLOSELY ASSOCIATED with a thing (but not literally part of it) to represent that thing — like 'the crown' standing for 'the king/monarchy' — that's METONYMY. When you use an actual PART of something to represent the WHOLE (or the whole to represent a part) — like 'hands' (a body part) standing for whole workers/people — that's SYNECDOCHE. Given that distinction, which term applies to 'the crown will decide', and which to 'all hands were needed'?

You've correctly matched both — well reasoned. Let's confirm fully: METONYMY substitutes a closely ASSOCIATED term for the thing itself without a part-whole relationship (crown = monarchy/kingship, by association). SYNECDOCHE specifically uses a PART to represent the WHOLE, or occasionally the whole to represent a part (hands = whole people, since a hand is literally a body part of each worker). The key test is always: is the substituted term an actual physical part of the thing (synecdoche), or merely something associated with it (metonymy)?
lit-0029: Say the word 'clang' out loud slowly. Does it just describe a metal sound, or does saying it actually sound a bit like metal striking metal?

Exactly — the word's sound imitates the thing it describes. Compare that to if the poet had instead written 'the hammer made a noise' — would that give you the same immediate sensory experience of being at the blacksmith's forge?
Right — so what is the specific term for words whose sound imitates the sound they describe, and what effect does it have on the reader's experience of the scene at the forge?
lit-0009: Think of a talking drum player at a festival — he doesn't just hit the drum randomly, he repeats a particular beat pattern to build a mood, maybe heaviness for mourning or urgency for war. Does the repeated pattern serve the mood, or is it just noise?
Right. Now say 'silent, sullen, suffering slaves' slowly to yourself — that repeated hard 's' sound — does it come out sounding light and quick, or heavy and drawn-out, almost like a hiss or a groan?
So if the repeated 's' sound physically forces the reader to slow down and produce something like a hiss or sigh, what mood or feeling about the slaves' condition might that sound be reinforcing?
lit-0049: Think of how 'moon' and 'lagoon' actually do rhyme fully at the end, but notice the word 'swoons' in the middle also shares that same 'oo' sound, even though it doesn't rhyme with anything at a line's end here. Is a shared vowel sound INSIDE a line the same as two words rhyming at the ends of separate lines?

Good distinction. Rhyme usually refers to matching end sounds across line endings, while a repeated vowel sound running through words within or across a line, without needing matching consonants after it, has its own separate name. Do you recall what that's called?
That's the correct term. So what musical or unifying effect might repeating that soft 'oo' sound across 'moon', 'swoons' and 'lagoon' have on how the line feels when read aloud?
lit-0064: Think of a political rally speaker who begins sentence after sentence with 'We will rebuild...', 'We will restore...', 'We will reclaim...'. Does repeating that same opening phrase make the speech feel weaker and more repetitive, or does it build momentum and conviction as it continues?

Exactly — repeated openings can build rhetorical force. Now in the poem's second stanza, does repeating 'We shall...' at the start of each line seem to build a similar mounting determination or resolve as the stanza progresses?
Good. What is the specific term for this device — repeating the same word or phrase at the START of successive lines — and how does it serve the stanza's overall tone of resolve?
lit-0054: Think of a native flute player who doesn't pause cleanly between musical phrases but lets one note bleed straight into the next, no clean breaks. Does that create a sense of smooth continuous flow, or does it sound broken and accidental?

Good parallel. Now, when a poetic line runs on into the next without a pause or punctuation, forcing you to read quickly onward to complete the thought, is that likely a printing accident, or a deliberate pacing choice by the poet?

Right — what is the technical term for a line running on into the next without a pause, and what effect might it create — urgency, breathlessness, or continuous flowing thought — at the specific point it occurs in this poem?
lit-0135: Think of school assembly. Before anything starts, the prefect shouts 'Assembly, attention!' and everyone stands straight. What does that call do before the announcements begin?
Exactly. Now in a moonlight tale in Yoruba land, the teller calls 'Alo o!' and the listeners reply 'Alo!' What do both sides show by that exchange?

Well put. These are called opening formulae, and many tales also have closing formulae. What would a closing formula do for the audience, and why might these formulae matter in oral performance more than in a written book?
lit-0136: Think of a church or mosque choir, or a football chant at the stadium. The leader shouts 'Super Eagles!' and the crowd replies 'Ooo-ooo!' What happens to the crowd when they reply together?

Right. So the pattern isn't just repeating words; it's about who is speaking. In the poem, one voice calls and a group answers. What does that tell you about the relationship between the leader and the community?
That's the heart of it: this is called call-and-response, a key feature of African oral poetry and song. How would that structure affect the mood of the poem when it's performed aloud?
lit-0137: Consider an age-grade meeting where a young member wants to collect the dues early. Instead of arguing, an elder says, 'The child who says his mother will not sleep will also not sleep.' Everyone goes quiet and nods. Why did the proverb win the argument better than a long explanation?

Correct. Now the business gave OUT goods in exchange, meaning value left the Sales side conceptually — in accounting, a sale is recorded as income leaving through the Sales account.
